subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to the law of reflection, the angle of incidence is equal to which angle?
options: The angle of reflection
The angle of refraction
The critical angle
The angle of the normal
questions.explain: The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

questions.q: In ray diagrams for reflection and refraction, angles are always measured relative to which line?
options: The normal
The reflecting surface
The horizontal
The principal axis
questions.explain: The normal is a line drawn at 90 degrees to the surface at the point where the ray meets it, and all angles are measured from it.

questions.q: Why does a rough surface such as paper produce a blurred, non-mirror image?
options: Diffuse reflection scatters rays in many directions
The light is completely absorbed
The light undergoes total internal reflection
The angle of incidence no longer equals the angle of reflection
questions.explain: A rough surface has normals pointing in many directions, so parallel rays are reflected in different directions, giving diffuse reflection.

questions.q: What is refraction?
options: The change in direction of light as it passes from one medium to another
The bouncing of light off a smooth surface
The splitting of white light into colours
The complete reflection of light inside a medium
questions.explain: Refraction is the bending of light as it crosses a boundary between media of different optical densities, caused by a change in its speed.

questions.q: When light passes from air into glass, which way does the ray bend?
options: Towards the normal
Away from the normal
Along the normal
Back into the air
questions.explain: Light slows down as it enters the glass, so it bends towards the normal (the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence).

questions.q: In CCEA Prescribed Practical P6, a graph of angle of incidence against angle of refraction for light entering a glass block shows that the two angles are...
options: related, but not directly proportional
directly proportional
always equal
not related to each other
questions.explain: As the angle of incidence increases, so does the angle of refraction, but the graph is a curve rather than a straight line through the origin, so they are related but not proportional.

questions.q: As light travels from air into an optically denser transparent material such as glass, what happens to its speed and frequency?
options: Speed decreases, frequency stays the same
Speed increases, frequency stays the same
Speed decreases, frequency decreases
Speed stays the same, frequency decreases
questions.explain: Light slows down in the glass and its wavelength shortens, but the frequency is unchanged.

questions.q: Light passes from air into a glass block at an angle of incidence of 50 degrees. Which of these could be the angle of refraction?
options: 30 degrees
50 degrees
70 degrees
90 degrees
questions.explain: Light slows down as it enters glass, so it bends towards the normal: the angle of refraction must be smaller than the 50 degree angle of incidence. Only 30 degrees fits.

questions.q: A ray of light inside a glass block reaches the glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees (less than the critical angle). What happens to the ray as it leaves the glass?
options: It speeds up and bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction is greater than 30 degrees
It slows down and bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is less than 30 degrees
It is totally internally reflected back into the glass
It carries straight on with no change of direction
questions.explain: Light travels faster in air than in glass, so on leaving the glass it speeds up and bends away from the normal: the angle of refraction in the air is larger than the angle of incidence.

questions.q: A ray hits a boundary along the normal (angle of incidence = 0 degrees). What happens?
options: It passes straight through without bending
It bends towards the normal
It bends away from the normal
It is totally internally reflected
questions.explain: At an angle of incidence of 0 degrees there is no change in direction, although the speed still changes.

questions.q: What is the critical angle?
options: The angle of incidence in the optically denser medium (e.g. glass) for which the angle of refraction in the air is 90 degrees
The angle at which light passes straight through unbent
The angle of incidence that equals the angle of reflection
The angle at which a lens focuses light
questions.explain: At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary at 90 degrees to the normal.

questions.q: Which two conditions are both required for total internal reflection to occur?
options: Light travels from an optically denser to a less dense medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
Light travels from a less dense to an optically denser medium AND the angle of incidence is below the critical angle
Light strikes the normal AND the medium is opaque
The angle of incidence is 0 degrees AND the medium is glass
questions.explain: TIR needs the light to be in the more optically dense medium and the angle of incidence to be greater than the critical angle.

questions.q: A ray of light inside a glass block meets the glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence smaller than the critical angle. What happens?
options: Most of the light refracts out into the air, bending away from the normal
All of the light is totally internally reflected
The refracted ray travels along the boundary
The light is absorbed by the glass
questions.explain: Below the critical angle the ray escapes into the air, refracting away from the normal (a little is also reflected). At the critical angle the refracted ray runs along the boundary, and above it the light is totally internally reflected.

questions.q: The critical angle for a type of glass is 42 degrees. A ray inside the glass meets the glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence of 60 degrees. What happens?
options: Total internal reflection: all the light is reflected back into the glass at 60 degrees to the normal
It refracts out into the air at an angle of refraction of 42 degrees
It refracts out into the air at an angle of refraction of 60 degrees
It travels along the glass-air boundary
questions.explain: 60 degrees is greater than the critical angle of 42 degrees, so no light escapes: it is totally internally reflected and, obeying the law of reflection, leaves the boundary at 60 degrees to the normal.

questions.q: Optical fibres are able to carry light signals over long distances mainly because of which process?
options: Total internal reflection
Diffuse reflection
Refraction into the surrounding air
Absorption of light
questions.explain: Light repeatedly undergoes total internal reflection along the fibre, so almost no light escapes through the sides.

questions.q: A right-angled glass prism (critical angle about 42 degrees) is used to turn a ray of light through 90 degrees. Why is total internal reflection used rather than a mirror?
options: The internal surface reflects almost all the light with no silvering needed
It bends the light towards the normal
It absorbs unwanted colours of light
It increases the speed of the light
questions.explain: At 45 degrees, which exceeds the critical angle, the prism reflects nearly 100 percent of the light, giving a brighter, sharper reflection than a silvered mirror.

questions.q: A converging lens has which shape?
options: Convex, thicker in the middle than at the edges
Concave, thinner in the middle than at the edges
Flat on both sides
Curved on one side only and always diverging
questions.explain: A converging (convex) lens is thickest at its centre and brings parallel rays together at the principal focus.

questions.q: What is the principal focus (focal point) of a converging lens?
options: The point where rays parallel to the principal axis converge after passing through the lens
The centre of the lens
The point where the object must be placed
The point where light is totally internally reflected
questions.explain: Rays parallel to the principal axis are refracted to meet at the principal focus, a distance of one focal length from the lens.

questions.q: What type of image does a diverging (concave) lens always produce of a real object?
options: Virtual, upright and diminished
Real, inverted and magnified
Real, upright and the same size
Virtual, inverted and magnified
questions.explain: A diverging lens always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image on the same side as the object.

questions.q: When a converging lens is used as a magnifying glass, where must the object be placed and what image is formed?
options: Closer than the focal length, giving a magnified, upright, virtual image
Beyond the focal length, giving a diminished, inverted, real image
Exactly at the focal length, giving an image at infinity
At twice the focal length, giving a same-size real image
questions.explain: With the object inside the focal length, a converging lens produces a magnified, upright, virtual image.

questions.q: A camera uses a converging lens to form an image of a distant tree on its sensor. Which of these describes the image?
options: Real, inverted and smaller than the tree
Virtual, upright and magnified
Real, upright and the same size as the tree
Virtual, inverted and smaller than the tree
questions.explain: A converging lens forms a real, inverted, diminished image of a distant object at (or just beyond) its principal focus - this is how a camera works, with the sensor (or film) placed where the real image forms.

questions.q: A student uses a converging lens to focus light from a distant window onto a screen. The image is sharpest when the screen is 15 cm from the lens. What is the focal length of the lens?
options: 15 cm
30 cm
7.5 cm
It cannot be found from this experiment
questions.explain: Rays from a distant object are almost parallel, so the lens brings them together at its principal focus. The lens-to-screen distance for a sharp image of a distant object is therefore the focal length: 15 cm.
